system.description:
The geisya can use one cantrip, as magic-users do. She names the cantrip she wants when she prays for the spell; everything else is as that cantrip's description. Most geisya choose legerdemain cantrips.

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

Cast on a small flame of the kind used for light. For the duration it can't be put out by normal means: snuffed underwater, in a strong wind or by cutting off the air, it relights at once. It doesn't work on a fire bigger than a small campfire.

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

The geisya throws a pinch of white powder into a fire (such as a brazier). It flashes brilliantly and makes a cloud of smoke of any color she likes, lasting the full duration. The smoke can take any simple, flat image she concentrates on; a geisya who specializes in painting can make instant artwork that fades when the spell ends. She isn't affected by the flash; onlookers who fail a save versus wands are blinded for 2-5 rounds.

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

The geisya scolds an attacking creature and thumps it with an ornamental fan. If it fails its saving throw, its aggression turns back on itself and it is stunned for 1-6 rounds. Only attacking, malicious, hungry or angry creatures are affected.

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

A protective spell. Her kimono, obi and tabi look the same but protect her as armor of AC 5 for the duration. Her dexterity bonus still applies, and her movement isn't hampered at all.

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

The geisya casts the first half with scarves at hand, and they vanish one by one: three scarves per level. She casts the second half (another two rounds) when they are to reappear, and can pull them from sleeves, from her audience's robes, from another geisya's ear and so on. They can be held in the spell's limbo for up to a day, after which they reappear around her on their own. While held they can't be detected, which makes the spell handy for passing secret messages.

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

The same as the 1st-level wu jen spell ventriloquism (see the OA Lite Spells compendium) except for its level and range.

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

The geisya thumps an attacker with an ornamental fan and scolds it. Unless it makes its saving throw, it loses all interest in attacking anything. If it is attacked, the spell is broken. It affects only creatures that thump can affect (attacking, malicious, hungry or angry ones).

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

Jest first works as the illusionist spell fascinate on everyone who hears it: those in the radius who fail their saving throw stop what they are doing and listen for the five segments of casting. When the spell is complete they get another saving throw. Failing it, they are helpless with laughter and can do nothing else for 1-10 rounds; attacking them at any time during the casting frees them. Those who make the second save simply walk away confused, unless attacked again, in which case they can fight back. A creature that fails the second save and isn't attacked while laughing sees the geisya as having a charisma of 20 for a full day. (The article also gives a comeliness of 20; OA Lite has no comeliness.)

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

Needs the juggling proficiency. The caster makes harmless balls of fire that can be juggled safely. With practice she can make other things instead: spheres of ice or water, colored balls of light or glowing white daggers, gaining one such choice for every three levels she has. The objects vanish when they touch anything but her hands, or when she stops concentrating. She can throw two a round at a target, which needs a missile hit roll for the target and one juggling roll to keep the rest in the air. Each does 1-4 damage +1 per level of the geisya, whatever its form, except the water ball, which does none.

Dragon #121 p.40-41 (Gregg Sharp, "The Geisya"). Rewritten in plain words.

rolls.label: Thrown object damage
rolls.note: Each object; the water ball does none.

system.description:
On the geisya list at 1st level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

The shukenja tries to learn whether some action in the next three turns will turn out well or badly. The chance of success is 70% plus 1% per level. The DM gives the answer, always in general terms; precise details are never revealed. Material component: a set of straight willow sticks or carved bones.

OA p.57; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

On the geisya list at 1st level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

Finds common things or forces of nature hidden from view: water, buried treasure, stolen goods and the like. The shukenja names what he seeks and holds a wand cut from a ginkgo tree (the material component) in both hands. If the thing is in range, the wand points toward it and pulls him along; if it meets an obstacle it can't pass (the ground, say), it presses against it and stops. If nothing matching is in range, the wand doesn't react, though he can move about searching.

OA p.58; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

On the geisya list at 1st level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

Foretells the general fortune of a major undertaking. The shukenja asks a deity for a sign about the plan; the casting itself is quick, but he must stay in one place watching the natural world around him for the whole casting time. Then he sees an omen (a flight of birds, an animal, a falling leaf) showing the undertaking's general fortune. It is often cast before a journey, a major battle or some notable feat.

  • The DM first weighs the plan against what only he knows. For example, the characters plan to leave a village to punish bandits in the mountains, but the DM knows the bandits will attack the village that night: an ill omen, since the characters wouldn't find the bandits.
  • With nothing to go on, he rolls 1d10 on Table 63 below (also the roll table "OA Table 63: Divination Results").
  • Omens are rare and hard to read, and the strain allows the spell only once a week.
d10Result
1-2Ill omen: the characters shouldn't undertake the task today. If they ignore the advice, all are -1 on to-hit and saving throw rolls for the rest of the day, their chance of encounters is doubled, and all encounters have a -10% reaction modifier.
3-4Great danger: the chance of encounters is doubled for the day, all encounters have a -10% reaction modifier, and foes are +1 to hit.
5-7Neutral omen: no special modifiers.
8-9Favorable omen: the characters can travel half again their normal rate today, and foes are -1 to hit them today.
10Auspicious omen: all the effects of a favorable omen, and +1 on all saving throws today.

OA Table 63: Divination Results.

OA p.58; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

On the geisya list at 1st level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Hardens the recipient against the pains and discomforts of heat, cold, fatigue and hunger.

  • Normal heat and cold don't affect him, and he takes 1 point less per die from magical fire and cold (ice, cold rays and so on).
  • Fatigue is banished as if he had slept an hour per level of the caster (this doesn't let spellcasters regain spells).
  • The effects of hunger and starvation are put off until the spell ends.

Material components: a piece of rice cake or dumpling, a scrap of cloth, a drop of water and an owl's feather.

OA p.59; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

On the geisya list at 2nd level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

Shows whether a creature is under a charm spell. Someone charmed by a creature gets a saving throw; if he succeeds, no charm is detected. The reverse shields one creature completely from this detection.

OA p.60; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

system.aoe: One animal within 3" radius of caster
system.description:
On the geisya list at 2nd level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

The shukenja can talk with any normal, non-fantastic warm- or cold-blooded creature of intelligence 1 or more. The animals don't attack while the spell lasts.

OA p.61; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

On the geisya list at 3rd level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

Gathers information about an area whose location is known: the relative strength of creatures there, the amount and value of treasure, and whether the area is watched by supernatural beings. The chance of a correct divination is 60% plus 1% per level, adjusted by the DM as needed; an incorrect divination gives wrong information. Material components: a handful of coins, incense and the shukenja's holy symbol; powerful divinations may need jewelry or magic items.

OA p.62; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

On the geisya list at 3rd level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

The caster can withstand normal fire and gets +2 on all saving throws against magical fire. For each level above 5th, he may affect one more man-sized creature (or equal mass). Material components: a powdered ruby and the shukenja's holy symbol.

OA p.63; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

On the geisya list at 4th level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

Foresees the general course of a character's life. The shukenja and the character must both be present, and important details of the character's life must be known (birth date, past deeds, family and so on). At the end, the shukenja predicts some major future event in the character's life. Neither of them has any control over the event; specific questions can't be asked or answered, and the exact circumstances (date, place and so on) aren't known. He can make only general statements.

  • The DM can decide the answer from an event he knows is coming: if he knows the character will soon anger a ninja clan, he might say "Soon your life will be full of danger from someone whose wrath you have earned. Expect danger from unexpected places and friendly strangers. Courage, cunning and caution should let you prevail."
  • Otherwise he rolls on Table 65 below (also the roll table "OA Table 65: Fate").
  • These fates are general, and many make good adventures: the DM notes the fate secretly and arranges for it to come about. He can also invent other fates.
  • A fate isn't absolute or unchangeable; it is a potential. The player's choices may change the outcome, and knowing his fate helps the character prepare to meet or avoid it.
  • A character has only one fate at a time. Once set, the nature of the event can't change, though the outcome can differ if his actions bring that about. A fate doesn't make him immune to death; he can die before it comes, especially by acting rashly or foolishly. In most cases, though, he should live to see it fulfilled, even if only for a few seconds.
d20Outcome
1He will overcome some great opponent in a valiant struggle.
2He will gain a great fortune but lose it before he can enjoy it.
3He will rise to high position and enjoy the respect and admiration of those around him.
4-5He will rise to high position, but evil scheming will bring about his fall.
6-7He will suffer a humiliating defeat at the hands of some great enemy.
8-9He will come into a great fortune that brings ruin and hardship to his house.
10-12Powerful beings will show him compassion, sparing his life at an unexpected moment.
13-15His family's actions will bring misfortune on him.
16-17A stranger will bring disguised good fortune into his life.
18He will win great favor with the mighty through a brave and heroic act.
19A stranger will bring ill fortune into his life.
20A fearful enemy will seek devious revenge on him when he least expects it.

OA Table 65: Fate.

Material components: incense, astrological charts and a silver gong.

OA p.65; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

On the geisya list at 4th level (Dragon #121, Table 1); otherwise as the OA shukenja spell.

The shukenja can speak the language of any creature in the area, including racial tongues and alignment languages. The reverse cancels tongues or confuses spoken communication.

OA p.67; geisya level from Dragon #121 p.40-41.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): A cleric can use it to soothe most kinds of mental distress except magical fear, which only remove fear cancels. No material component.

The OA shukenja spell calm (OA p.57), for reference:

Soothes a mind troubled by fear, temporary insanity, confusion or other mental distress, ending the effect and restoring the recipient's normal state of mind. The shukenja points at the recipient and recites a few holy scriptures. Because his distress makes him unwilling, the recipient saves versus spell: if he saves, the spell fails; if he fails, he is calmed. Material component: a prayer wheel or a page of sutras.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.57. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): No material component.

The OA shukenja spell detect disease (OA p.58), for reference:

Shows whether a creature (or object) carries a disease, normal or magical, with a 10% chance per level of identifying the exact disease. Material component: a bamboo wand with paper strips inscribed with prayers.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): The material component is the cleric's holy symbol.

The OA shukenja spell detect harmony (OA p.58), for reference:

Gives general information on the balance of forces (good, evil, law and chaos) in an area: not the exact alignment or nature of anything, only the general proportions. The DM answers from what he knows of the target, always vaguely ("there is more evil than good here", "the lawful order of the universe is strong here").

  • On a living creature, it counts not just its alignment but its deeds, its present intentions and anything else at odds with its stated alignment: a lawful evil character known for occasional bursts of compassion for the helpless might read as "faithful, but with the other forces at struggle".
  • On buildings and areas, it shows whether powers are at work there: a house haunted by spirits leans toward evil and destruction; the cave of a famous holy hermit gives the opposite impression.

Material component: a specially prepared scroll of sutras costing 25 gp for paper and inks.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): Second level for most clerics; a deity whose sphere includes divination and fortune telling may grant it as a 1st-level spell.

The OA shukenja spell omen (OA p.58), for reference:

Foretells the general fortune of a major undertaking. The shukenja asks a deity for a sign about the plan; the casting itself is quick, but he must stay in one place watching the natural world around him for the whole casting time. Then he sees an omen (a flight of birds, an animal, a falling leaf) showing the undertaking's general fortune. It is often cast before a journey, a major battle or some notable feat.

10Auspicious omen: all the effects of a favorable omen, and +1 on all saving throws today.

OA Table 63: Divination Results.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): Material components: a quill from an eagle's feather and ink made from dragon's blood. The foe's identity and several prayers of the cleric's religion are written on the weapon with them, as for the shukenja spell.

The OA shukenja spell weapon bless (OA p.59), for reference:

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Prepares one weapon to fight a particular foe. The shukenja carefully writes on the weapon who the foe is, with several sutras to give it power. He needn't know the foe's name, but must identify one specific character or creature: "a kappa" isn't enough, but "the kappa who lives in Ch'i Sheng's millpond" is.

  • The weapon is then +5 to hit and damage on its first attack against that foe, and counts as magical for hitting creatures harmed only by magical weapons.
  • It doesn't add to a magical weapon's bonus: on a +2 weapon the effect is still +5, not +7.
  • If the weapon strikes another creature while the spell lasts, the blade is wiped clean and the spell is lost.

Material component: a writing brush and ink made from dragon's blood.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.59. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA shukenja spell castigate (OA p.62), for reference:

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

A blasting rebuke on the shukenja's foes, its effect depending on each victim's alignment compared with his:

  • Same alignment: save versus spell or be deafened for 1-3 rounds by his blistering words.
  • One part different (law, neutrality, chaos, good or evil): 1 point of damage per level of the caster, or 1/2 point per level on a successful save versus spell.
  • Both parts different: 1-4 points per level of the caster, half on a successful save.

So a lawful good shukenja deafens lawful good victims, does 1 point per level to lawful neutral, lawful evil, chaotic good and neutral good, and 1-4 per level to true neutral, neutral evil, chaotic neutral and chaotic evil. Material component: the shukenja's holy symbol.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): Material components: a small gem worth at least 10 gp and a few fresh rose petals.

The OA shukenja spell detect curse (OA p.62), for reference:

The shukenja has a 5% chance per level of detecting any cursed item, person or place. He can check one man-sized object or one square yard of area each round. Once a cursed item is found, he has the same chance of learning the general nature of the curse, though not its exact triggers and effects: scanning a cursed scroll, he might learn that it brings the reader misfortune, but not that it lowers the reader's saving throws and to-hit rolls by 1 until removed. He can check each item or area only once, however many times he casts the spell. Material components: a gem worth at least 10 gp (given to his deity as an offering) and a fresh spray of cherry or plum blossoms.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): Affects only ordinary, nonmagical snakes; no serpents or serpentlike creatures come. Material components: the cleric's holy symbol and a miniature silver flute, which vanishes when the spell is cast.

The OA shukenja spell snake summoning (OA p.61), for reference:

Calls all snakes, serpents and serpent-like creatures in the area. Creatures with more hit dice than the shukenja's level, or with high intelligence, save versus spell to avoid it. Those who fail (or get no save) come to the shukenja and follow him while he keeps concentrating, and don't try to harm him or those with him unless attacked; an attack breaks the spell. He can move at half speed without breaking concentration. At the end, the serpents return to their normal state, with whatever results that brings. Material component: a small silver flute, played for the whole duration.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.61. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): Deities with little regard for healing or protection (notably war gods, barbarian deities and death gods) don't grant it. The prepared statue must be made from materials costing at least 25 gp.

The OA shukenja spell substitution (OA p.64), for reference:

The shukenja transfers a limited amount of his damage to a specially prepared figure of his deity.

  • First he must personally make a statue of his deity from materials worth at least 25 gp, and each casting needs an offering suited to the deity.
  • Each casting lets the statue absorb 1-4 hit points of damage he takes, wherever he is. This happens automatically: the first damage he takes goes to the statue.
  • Repeated castings on the same statue can transfer up to 20 hit points. He can never have more than one substitution in effect at a time.
  • Absorbed damage leaves no mark on him but shows on the statue. The statue can't be healed; once all its points are used, a new statue must be made.
  • The spell comes from the shukenja's great faith and service, as an act of compassion from his deity; one in questionable standing with his deity can never use it.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.64. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): Treated as a 3rd-level improved find traps rather than a 2nd-level spell that partly repeats it: the chance to detect any mechanical or magical trap within the 10-foot radius rises to 100%, and to detect any other danger (including invisible opponents) to 50%. Casting time 6 segments. Otherwise as the shukenja spell.

The OA shukenja spell warning (OA p.62), for reference:

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Sharpens the recipient's awareness of danger.

  • His chance of being surprised by events within the area drops by one (1-2 in 6 becomes 1 in 6, and so on). A missile shot from outside the area can still surprise him.
  • Within the same limits he can't be struck from behind, since he is automatically aware of anything moving behind him.
  • 30% chance he automatically notices any trap or hidden danger (including invisible foes) in the area.
  • Any foe in the area has half the normal chance to hide in shadows or move silently.

Only the recipient notices the warnings; it is up to him whether to tell the rest of his group. Material component: a small metal figure sprinkled with the dust of a crushed pearl.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): A new spell, like the shukenja's detect shapechanger but detecting any lycanthrope. Cast on one in human form, it shows the person is a lycanthrope but not which kind; cast on one in animal form, it shows the creature is a lycanthrope but not its human identity. Material component: a balm of honey, dried carrot, moonwort and belladonna rubbed on the caster's eyelids. Range, duration, area of effect and casting time as detect shapechanger.

The OA shukenja spell detect shapechanger (OA p.65), for reference:

The shukenja sees the true form of any shapechanger: the shape the creature most often takes. If it is in that form now, the spell shows that it is a shapechanger, but not its other possible forms. It doesn't reveal the kind of shapechanger or its alignment or intentions. One creature or one square yard of area can be examined each round. Material component: a balm of honey and lotus flower smeared on the caster's eyelids.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.65. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): The material component for the reverse, fatigue, is a little cumin seed or poison nut.

The OA shukenja spell endurance (OA p.65), for reference:

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Banishes fatigue from lack of sleep and overexertion, filling the recipient with energy and vigor. For someone who has gone without rest, it is as if he had had eight hours of restful sleep in the last 24: he could be active for 24 hours (out of need), grow fatigued, receive this spell and be fully functional at once. For someone already well rested, it removes the need for sleep for the next 24 hours. It doesn't restore spells. It affects one character for every two levels of the caster.

The reverse, fatigue, tires the victim as if he hadn't slept in 24 hours: -2 to hit, -1 on all saving throws, and 2/3 normal movement. If he doesn't rest within 12 hours, he collapses from exhaustion and sleeps 10 hours; if sleep is impossible, he can take no effective action. Eight hours of rest (before collapse) cancels it. The victim saves versus spell to avoid it.

Material component: a pinch of sand (a small noisemaker for fatigue).

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.65. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): Clerics of any alignment can cast it on opponents of any alignment to force them into a desired behavior. A chaotic cleric is less likely than a lawful or neutral one to keep to the terms of the oath.

The OA shukenja spell oath (OA p.63), for reference:

The shukenja tries to force a deed or behavior on an unwilling creature in return for some consideration from him (usually sparing its life). The creature must understand his speech.

  • The oath must be limited to things the creature can do with its natural abilities, and can't directly cause harm to it or another. He could make a highwayman swear never to rob again, an evil monster return to the deserted lands it came from, or a lord never again overtax his peasants; he couldn't demand that a monster kill itself, or force a samurai to attack a camp of dangerous monsters. The DM decides whether an oath goes beyond these limits.
  • The victim saves versus spell to avoid it, at -2 if he was subdued in combat.
  • Once in effect, both sides freely choose whether to keep the terms. If the shukenja (or anyone with him) breaks the oath, the creature is freed at once. If the victim tries to break the terms, he is struck with racking pains, losing 1 hit point a round until he gives in or dies.
  • Oaths can be removed by the reverse, unbind, or by atonement.

Material component (oath and unbind): the shukenja's holy symbol.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.63. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA shukenja spell pacify (OA p.66), for reference:

The shukenja recites a few fitting sutras, bringing a still calm over the area. Everyone in it is pacified, unable to attack or harm others.

  • Spells and weapons that would directly or potentially harm others can't be used.
  • Those affected can't physically block other creatures' movement, though they can barricade exits or stand in the way.
  • If the area holds more creatures than he can affect, those with the fewest hit dice are affected first.
  • If an affected creature is attacked by someone unaffected, the spell ends at once for that creature, with no loss of initiative, since it can clearly see others' hostile intent.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.66. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): Material components: the cleric's holy symbol, burning incense and the cleric's prayer vestment.

The OA shukenja spell reanimation (OA p.66), for reference:

Revives a recently dead character (dead no more than 24 hours) into a half-life, neither dead nor fully alive. He must make a system shock roll for it to work (though this costs no constitution); if he succeeds, he has 1 hit point.

  • He can't fight or use magic items, has no spells memorized and can't regain any, but can move and speak: movement is half normal and speech slow and slurred.
  • His memory is cloudy and confused, and he has trouble remembering even basic details of his past life and friends. Left unwatched, he tends to wander off aimlessly, with no idea where he is going or has been.
  • He can be slain again (and reanimated again if necessary). He needs no food, sleep or drink.
  • Raise dead, resurrection, limited wish or wish returns him to normal.

Material components: a strip of white cloth inscribed with prayers, the shukenja's holy symbol and a stick of incense.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.66. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): Material components: a few drops of wine and a small piece of bread.

The OA shukenja spell sustain (OA p.67), for reference:

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

The shukenja, or the creature it is cast on, can go without food or water for the duration without suffering starvation or thirst, though he can eat and drink normally. Afterward he resumes normal eating and drinking with no ill effect from the time without food. Cast on a creature already suffering from starvation and thirst, it counts as one filling meal for every six hours of duration. Material components: a flask of warm sake and a rice cake.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.67. Rewritten in plain words.

Cleric version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA shukenja spell advice (OA p.67), for reference:

The shukenja gives profound, thoughtful advice to any creature of at least low intelligence with whom he shares a language. The creature saves versus spell to avoid it. If it fails, he can give it instructions in the form of advice, to do anything, including obviously foolish or self-destructive things, and it does its best to obey.

  • If the advice would put it in great danger or cause its death, it gets a second save versus spell at +4 just before doing it: told to jump off a nearby cliff (and unable to fly), it saves just before the fatal step.
  • It doesn't hide who gave the advice, and bad advice can bring the shukenja trouble if those who follow it survive.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.67. Rewritten in plain words.

The OA wu jen spell warp stone (OA p.92), for reference:

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

Like warp wood: natural stone buckles and bends as if it were plastic. Walls buckle, stone doors burst their fittings, pillars bend and statues twist. The DM decides the exact effect from the kind of structure and the amount of stone. Material component: a piece of clay twisted in the caster's hands.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.92. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): A quill from a hawk's feather replaces the brush for writing the mystic character on each missile.

The OA wu jen spell accuracy (OA p.74), for reference:

Temporarily enchants missiles, normal or magical, so they hit distant targets more easily. It works on anything a normal man-sized creature can shoot or throw: a bundle of arrows, yes; a ballista bolt, no. A stone thrown by a giant isn't affected, nor is a boulder thrown by someone wearing a girdle of giant strength.

  • The missile glows faintly, easy to tell from normal missiles.
  • For the duration, all its range categories are doubled: an arrow from a daikyu has ranges of 14" (short), 28" (medium) and 42" (long) instead of 7", 14" and 21". This makes it more accurate, since the range modifiers may be smaller than they would otherwise be.
  • The enchantment stays on the missile until the duration ends, so a missile shot at a foe could be shot back if easily found.

The reverse, inaccuracy, is cast on a creature, not a missile. For the duration, all missiles shot at it count as one range category farther away: short becomes medium, medium becomes long, and long targets are out of range.

Material components: brush and ink, used to write a mystic character on each missile enchanted. The reverse needs a thick piece of ground glass.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.74. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell chameleon (OA p.75), for reference:

The recipient's coloring changes to match the background. Moving through gradually changing surroundings (from a forest's edge into a green field), it changes automatically; an abrupt change (from forest to a gray stone wall) takes a round. He blends into his surroundings and is hard to spot and attack.

  • Beyond 10", he can't be spotted (though he can be seen if someone standing closer points him out).
  • Closer, he counts as having a 20% chance to hide in shadows, without needing to stay still. Characters who can already hide in shadows get +20% if they stay still.
  • Missile weapons are -4 to hit him.

Material component: the shed skin of a small lizard.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.75. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell secret signs (OA p.76), for reference:

Creates a secret means of communication between the wu jen and one other intelligent creature, named when the spell is cast, who must be within sight and hearing. With one gesture, sound or even the placing of an object, the caster passes on a complete thought of 25 words or less, understood regardless of language (though interpreting it is another matter): waving his hand in the air to say "Come see me when all are asleep", or placing a scroll on a table to say "Leave now and wait for me to contact you". The recipient must clearly see and hear the wu jen. There is no set component, since the component is whatever means sends the message, so it can be used even when the wu jen is bound and gagged. It can't be used to trigger or deliver other spells.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.76. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell swim (OA p.77), for reference:

Element: Water (OA Table 66).

The recipient swims as easily as a fish, at 12", carrying his normal load with no trouble. A normally outfitted character can't drown while it lasts, though excess weight still makes him sink and drown normally. It doesn't let him breathe underwater.

The reverse, sinking, lowers the target's swimming ability by one class unless he saves versus spell: natural swimmers count as land creatures trained in swimming, those with the swimming proficiency count as without it, and those without it sink like stones. Material component (either): the scale of a goldfish.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.77. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell prestidigitation (OA p.76), for reference:

Sharpens the wu jen's manual dexterity and lets him teleport small objects to other points on his body.

  • Picking pockets: the victim saves versus spell. If he saves, the attempt is discovered, with whatever consequences follow; if he fails, the wu jen takes the item.
  • Palming: with a quick pass of the hand, things small enough to fit in his palm vanish and reappear elsewhere on his person (a pocket, a boot, the other hand), or come from elsewhere on his person into his hand. Onlookers save versus spell to notice.
  • Each trick takes only seconds, and several can be done in one round: he could pick up a rare gem, secretly move it to his hat and replace it with a cheap substitute from his pocket in a few seconds.

Material component: a small drop of oil rubbed on the fingertips.

The reverse, fumble-fingers, is cast on a victim within 3". For the duration, he must save versus spell to perform any action needing manual dexterity. It doesn't affect large actions such as melee, but can make an archer fumble his arrow, a ninja drop his tools, or a spellcaster confuse his gestures. Material component: a little oil sprinkled at the victim.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.76. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell protection from charm (OA p.80), for reference:

The recipient gets +1 for every three levels of the wu jen on any saving throw against charm magic, including spells and spell-like effects. It doesn't help against attacks that allow no save. Material component: a piece of a charming creature, or hair from a character of exceptional beauty.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.80. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell (one level higher for magic-users).

The OA wu jen spell still water (OA p.77), for reference:

Element: Water (OA Table 66).

Calms even the most turbulent water (except tsunami force) for the duration: stormy seas become smooth, raging rapids subside, flood waters flow calmly. It changes the water's rate of flow and the force of its movement to a gentle flow: whirlpools and turbulent rapids become a gentle stream easily crossed. It doesn't change the amount of water passing through, only its force.

  • Cast on a water elemental or other creature of the Elemental Plane of Water (or of watery substance), the target saves versus spell. On a success, nothing happens; on a failure, it can't take directly hostile actions, though it can still cause harm indirectly. If such a becalmed creature is attacked, the spell ends at once.

Material component: a tiny flask of whale oil.

The reverse, turbulence, makes water choppier: still water becomes whitecapped and choppy; whitecaps become strong waves able to capsize canoes and small boats; stormy ocean becomes huge, mounting waves able to swamp small ships. Cast on water elementals or similar creatures, it makes them hostile and belligerent. Material component: a small ornamental fan.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.77. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell animate fire (OA p.81), for reference:

Element: Fire (OA Table 66).

The wu jen controls the movement of normal fire: flames leap at an opponent, spread in a chosen direction, flare up into the sky or sink to a quiet smolder. The fire can move any way he likes (at 3"), if there is fuel for it. He can also make it burn hotter, doing double normal damage while using up its fuel twice as fast. His level sets how much fire he can animate, and how far flames can reach from the main fire: a 9th level wu jen can make a flame reach 9 feet from the main body of the fire. He must concentrate; if his concentration breaks, the spell ends. Material components: a handful of charcoal, sulfur and soda ash.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.81. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell (one level higher for magic-users).

The OA wu jen spell animate water (OA p.78), for reference:

Element: Water (OA Table 66).

Animates any amount of water up to the area of effect. The wu jen can't shape it, but can make it flow in any direction, at 6" a round while he concentrates. It is still subject to evaporation, absorption and gravity: fire and heat quickly finish it off, and earth turns to mud, drawing off most of it. It can climb gentle slopes, but walls, stairs and other abrupt rises stop it. Used to attack, it crashes into opponents as a wave, doing 1-2 points of damage per 1/2" cube of water animated. While concentrating he can move up to 3" but take no other actions; if his concentration breaks, the spell ends. Material component: a small vial of pure spring water mixed with cinnabar ore.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.78. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): A new spell, the same as the 4th-level cleric spell detect lycanthrope (see the Cleric folder).

The OA shukenja spell detect shapechanger (OA p.65), for reference:

The shukenja sees the true form of any shapechanger: the shape the creature most often takes. If it is in that form now, the spell shows that it is a shapechanger, but not its other possible forms. It doesn't reveal the kind of shapechanger or its alignment or intentions. One creature or one square yard of area can be examined each round. Material component: a balm of honey and lotus flower smeared on the caster's eyelids.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.65. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell magnetism (OA p.83), for reference:

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

Has two uses, chosen when cast.

  • On himself: he can draw iron and steel items in the area to his hand on command, one item per round. A creature holding the item saves versus spell to resist; he can try again on the same item in a later round. He could snatch weapons from others' grasp, or turn arrows in flight. If the item has more mass than he does, the effect reverses and he is drawn to it: trying to draw a man in metal armor usually drags the wu jen to him, not always a good result. It is strong enough to pull him through the air, a good way of crossing a chasm if there is enough iron on the other side.
  • On another: the victim saves versus spell to avoid it. If he fails, all iron and steel within 3" of him is drawn to him; items held by creatures get the same saving throw as above, and if an item has more mass than the target, the movement reverses.
  • Either way, weapons drawn by the spell do no damage, since no conscious mind wields or controls them.

Material component: a piece of lodestone. The reverse, demagnetize, ends a magnetism; its component is a small wooden rod.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.83. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): Material components: a quill from an owl's feather, a pot of ink and a sheet of vellum.

The OA wu jen spell memory (OA p.83), for reference:

Plants a false memory in the mind of an intelligent creature that understands the wu jen's speech. The victim saves versus spell, at -2 if unconscious or asleep.

  • After the brief casting, the wu jen goes on describing the memory. He can implant memories of events up to 1 turn long per level: a 12th level wu jen could build a memory of an event two hours long. The exact casting time is however long the description takes.
  • He gains limited knowledge of the victim's existing memories, only enough to fit the new one logically into the flow of events.
  • The new memory can replace one already there (changing how an encounter turned out, or the orders the victim received), or be wedged into a "blank space" (an encounter during an otherwise forgettable journey).
  • It has no magical force (it isn't a suggestion), but can be used to encourage friendliness or hostility, or change the victim's mission. The wu jen must take care to make memories logical, fitting the victim's personality or logically explained: telling an intelligent evil monster it likes a traditional enemy of its race simply because he was nice isn't enough; telling it that it likes the character because he spared its life is far more acceptable. If the DM rules the memory wholly out of character, the victim gets a second save at +4 at the end of the spell.

The reverse, erasement, removes any memory from the victim, with the same limits. The time erased is a blank to him; he has no idea what happened.

Dispel magic, remember or a similar spell removes an implanted memory or restores an erased one. Material components: a sheet of white paper, a brush and a pot of ink.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.83. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): No material component. (4th level because magic-users cast remove curse at that level.)

The OA shukenja spell detect curse (OA p.62), for reference:

The shukenja has a 5% chance per level of detecting any cursed item, person or place. He can check one man-sized object or one square yard of area each round. Once a cursed item is found, he has the same chance of learning the general nature of the curse, though not its exact triggers and effects: scanning a cursed scroll, he might learn that it brings the reader misfortune, but not that it lowers the reader's saving throws and to-hit rolls by 1 until removed. He can check each item or area only once, however many times he casts the spell. Material components: a gem worth at least 10 gp (given to his deity as an offering) and a fresh spray of cherry or plum blossoms.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): Elementals save at +2, since magic-users are less skilled with elements and elementals than wu jen.

The OA wu jen spell elemental turning (OA p.85), for reference:

Element: All (OA Table 66).

A fearsome spell, the bane of elementals, drives them off. The wu jen must choose the kind of elemental before casting. Every elemental of that kind in the area saves versus spell: if it saves, it can ignore the spell; if it fails, it flees the area and doesn't re-enter it for the duration. The area is centered on the wu jen and moves with him. An elemental forced into a position where it can't escape the area vanishes to its own plane. It doesn't break the concentration of anyone else controlling the elemental. Material component: a pinch of the element opposed to the kind turned: fire for water elementals, earth for air, a puff of breath for earth, a drop of water for fire.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.85. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): Material component: a ruby chip worth at least 100 gp.

The OA wu jen spell melt metal (OA p.86), for reference:

Element: Fire (OA Table 66).

A gentle touch sends a charge of fiery magic energy from the wu jen's fingertip into a normal metal item, making it so hot that it melts and flows at one cubic inch per round. Bars and locks are easily cut free. He must concentrate on focusing the energy and can do nothing else. It affects only normal metal items. Material component: a gem worth at least 100 gp.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.86. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell quell (OA p.86), for reference:

The wu jen points at the target and speaks a few mystic words, trying to subdue him at once. The victim must be intelligent, but needn't understand the caster's language. He saves versus spell; if he fails, he surrenders at once, just as if subdued in combat.

  • The wu jen can also demand some service of the subdued creature, if it understands his speech. It gets a second save versus spell; if it succeeds, the quell is broken. If it fails, it agrees to the service and tries to complete it.
  • The service can be anything that doesn't cause the creature's death or injury and has a hope of success in a short time. It won't leap into a fire (unless immune to fire), but will risk dashing into a burning building to save someone or something, since it has a reasonable chance of success.
  • It uses the safest, easiest, most efficient way, preparing as well as its intelligence allows: in that example it would probably soak itself and wrap up in wet blankets first (if smart enough to think of it).
  • When the service is done, it is free of the quell, and if it feels strong enough, may seek revenge on the caster as soon as the spell lifts. If the service has no set end ("guard and protect me"), it gets a new save each day to break the spell, at +2 if the caster and his friends seem especially weakened.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.86. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): Duration only 4 turns per level of the caster.

The OA wu jen spell reverse flow (OA p.86), for reference:

Reverses the flow of any body of water in the area: a stream or river runs upstream, an ocean current flows the other way, even a waterfall falls upward. The change of direction has no ill effect on the water. Its main use is helping ships travel against the current or upstream, but it also reverses pumps, drains water traps and the like. The reverse returns water to its normal flow.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.86. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell transfix (OA p.87), for reference:

A more powerful hold person. The wu jen picks the center of the effect, and every creature in the area at that moment saves versus spell; those who fail are transfixed, unable to move, speak, cast spells or act.

  • The wu jen must then state a condition that releases them ("Wait here until I return", "Stay there for all eternity!"). It can be anything, however unlikely; when it is met, they are released automatically.
  • Every six turns they remain transfixed, they get another save versus spell to escape.
  • Creatures entering the area after the casting also save versus spell (at +4) or are transfixed, each time they enter. Creatures removed from the area are freed at once.
  • The spell stays active as long as at least one creature is transfixed.

Material component: a barnacle crushed underfoot when the spell is cast, or a drop of pine resin.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.87. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell wood shape (OA p.84), for reference:

Element: Nature (OA Table 66).

The wu jen shapes natural wood into any form he likes. As with smoke shape, the detail is rough and crude, but enough to fool at a distance: doors can be made in wooden walls, or a chest from a tree trunk. Once made, the shape is permanent unless destroyed by fire, rot or chopping. It doesn't make the material light or easy to move; the wu jen needs help moving larger things into place. Material component: a miniature carpenter's adze.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.84. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell ironwood (OA p.88), for reference:

Element: Nature (OA Table 66).

Gives wood the strength of the finest steel. Only its hardness changes; color, texture and weight are unaffected. Cast on normal living plants, it has a 50% chance of working; if it does, it doesn't interfere with normal growth, but every part of the plant (leaves, flowers and fruit included) has the hardness of steel. A plant-like monster saves versus spell; if it fails, it becomes rigid and paralyzed, its armor class becomes 0, and a to-hit roll is always needed to strike it, since the hardness runs through its whole body. Material component: a pinch of metal filings mixed with willow sap.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.88. Rewritten in plain words.

system.aoe: 1 cubic foot/level within a 10' sq. area
system.description:
Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell mass (OA p.88), for reference:

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

Controls the weight of an item within the size limit, making it too heavy to move or light as a feather; the wu jen can raise it one round and lower it the next, at will. Mass can be raised or lowered by up to 5% per level: at 10th level, by 50%. It doesn't otherwise change the item. Several items in the same 10-foot square can be affected. Missiles can be made up to twice as heavy (doing double normal damage) and still be shot, but their ranges are halved. Heavy things can be carried easily, though bulk may still prevent it: a huge boulder made very light is still hard to carry because of its size. Material components: a hummingbird's feather and a bit of an elephant's toenail.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.88. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA shukenja spell mental strength (OA p.68), for reference:

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Fortifies the mind of the shukenja or another: +4 on saving throws against spells and magical effects that work on the will (illusions, enchantments, charms, hypnosis, suggestion, fear, possession, telepathic attacks and so on). Against mental attacks that normally allow no save (pacify and so on), the recipient saves on 17 or better to avoid the effect. The reverse, mental weakness, does the opposite, lowering saving throws against mental attacks by 4; the victim must be touched but gets no save. Material component: the tail of a fox.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.68. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell metal skin (OA p.88), for reference:

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

The skin of a creature touched becomes a gleaming, steel-hard surface: its armor class becomes 2 for the duration, but it grows slow and stiff, moving at half speed and always acting last in combat. Its skin counts as metal for the magnetism spell. Material component: a small piece of rhinoceros hide, swallowed by the caster.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.88. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): Casting time 5 segments.

The OA wu jen spell servant horde (OA p.89), for reference:

Creates 2d6 +1 per level invisible servants like unseen servant, with all its limits, except that they can also do common labor if carefully directed by the caster: serve at a banquet, help dig earthworks, row a ship, act as porters, or help in a farmer's fields. Material component: a small stick crossbar hung with many lengths of knotted thread.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.89. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell water to poison (OA p.90), for reference:

Element: Nature/Water (OA Table 66).

Turns water (or any drinkable liquid) into a poison that does 1d4 per level of the caster, half on a successful save versus poison. One swallow is enough. Those smelling the liquid have a 1% chance per level of experience of noticing the poison. Diluted to as little as 50% strength, it does proportionally less damage; diluted further, it only makes drinkers slightly ill. The reverse, poison to water, does the opposite. Material component: the fang of a poisonous snake, dissolved in the liquid to be poisoned or purified.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.90. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): Casting time 5 segments.

The OA wu jen spell wood rot (OA p.90), for reference:

Element: Nature (OA Table 66).

A sickly pale fire leaps from the caster's fingertips and dances over the wooden target.

  • On a live plant, it works 75% of the time. A plant-like creature saves versus spell to resist. Nonliving wooden things get no save.
  • Once it takes effect, the wood decays at 1 cubic foot per turn; plant-like creatures lose 1 hit die per cubic foot rotted. The rotted wood falls away, crumbling at a touch, until the whole object has rotted. A wooden door can be destroyed in several turns; a large wooden building takes several days.

The reverse, prevent rot, stops the decay caused by wood rot, but doesn't restore wood already decayed. Material component: a live termite (dead, for the reverse).

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.90. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell aura (OA p.90), for reference:

Reads the aura of an area: the basic alignment and magical tendencies of most of its inhabitants and things. An aura appears over every dwelling or structure in the area, showing whether most of its occupants, or the main one, are good, evil, lawful, neutral or chaotic; areas with a high concentration of magic are shown too. Standing on a hill above a village, the wu jen sees each house glow with the nature of those inside, telling good people, evildoers and lawful folk apart. Temples and shrines glow with magic, since they are more inclined to it, and haunted and cursed places have a fitting aura. It even appears over dwellings the caster can't see directly: a faint glow above the treetops might show a hut or cave deep in the woods. The reverse, mask, hides the aura of one dwelling from this spell.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.90. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell gambler's luck (OA p.90), for reference:

The wu jen has no control over what form this takes; he must abide by the winds of fate. 60% chance the result is good, 40% bad.

  • Good: every die roll for the character improves by 1 (or 10% for percentile rolls) for the duration.
  • Bad: his die rolls aren't affected, but he is gripped by a gambling mania for the duration. He automatically accepts any game of chance or wager offered him that has some element of chance (dares don't count). It doesn't force him to accept suicidal bets (he won't agree to kill himself, or let himself be killed, on a coin toss), but he would accept a bet offering freedom or surrender on a roll of the die. He keeps playing any game until he can't pay, though he tries to borrow from others to stay in.

Material component: a small statuette of the god of luck.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.90. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell metal to rust (OA p.91), for reference:

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

With a single touch, ferrous metal crumbles into a pile of rust. The wu jen touches the item (rolling to hit if needed), and it falls away in large flakes. Normal metal items get no save; magical metals save versus disintegration (17 for hard metal, 19 for soft metal and jewelry), with a bonus for the strength of their magic. Magic items of iron without a set plus (an iron amulet of ESP, say) get a bonus set by the DM. The reverse, rust to metal, restores a rusted item if at least 90% of the original material is there. Material component: a flask of seawater.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.91. Rewritten in plain words.

system.aoe: Hit dice or levels equal to caster's
system.description:
Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell pain (OA p.91), for reference:

Aimed at one or more creatures, all within 20 feet of each other. All are struck by pain and agony that passes in an instant, but leaves their muscles knotted and their strength lowered: dexterity and strength drop to 3 for 2d4 rounds, giving -3 to hit, -1 damage, -3 on reaction and attacking adjustment, and +4 to defensive adjustment (worse armor class). Then they return to normal. Strength or prestidigitation ends it, giving the vitality needed to restore normal strength and dexterity. Material components: a leech, and a stone scraped against a slate.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.91. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): As the OA spell.

The OA wu jen spell warp stone (OA p.92), for reference:

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

Like warp wood: natural stone buckles and bends as if it were plastic. Walls buckle, stone doors burst their fittings, pillars bend and statues twist. The DM decides the exact effect from the kind of structure and the amount of stone. Material component: a piece of clay twisted in the caster's hands.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.92. Rewritten in plain words.

Magic-User version (Dragon #130): The elemental's task can take no longer than one day per two levels of the magic-user.

The OA wu jen spell elemental servant (OA p.93), for reference:

Summons one of the four kinds of elementals (earth, air, fire or water) and compels it to do a service. Halfway through the casting, a 16 hit die elemental of the right kind appears and the caster states the service.

  • The service must be within the elemental's powers, take no more than one day per level of the wu jen, and be done within its own element: water elementals won't do work that takes them onto land, and fire elementals must stay in their fiery realms.
  • If it saves versus spell, it vanishes at once back to its own plane. If it fails, it tries to carry out the mission. The wu jen needn't supervise; they agree to meet at some set place when it is done.
  • Typical services: a fire elemental forging a blade in the heat of a volcano, a water elemental recovering things from the bottom of the ocean, an earth elemental bringing rare ores from deep in the earth, an air elemental carrying the wu jen somewhere.
  • Once the mission is done and the meeting kept, it returns at once to its plane. Elementals resent being summoned and forced to serve, and may try to take revenge later.

Material components: a large quantity of the element, and a written document stating exactly what service is to be done.

Turns the recipient's face into a horrible, terrifying mask, with nearly any mix of hideous features the caster likes: blue skin, a parrot face, an elephant's nose, rotting tusks. He can't copy the look of a known creature, though parts of different creatures can be combined into something new.

  • It startles the unprepared and those of little experience: opponents' surprise rolls go up by 1 where surprise is rolled.

The OA wu jen spell chameleon (OA p.75), for reference:

The recipient's coloring changes to match the background. Moving through gradually changing surroundings (from a forest's edge into a green field), it changes automatically; an abrupt change (from forest to a gray stone wall) takes a round. He blends into his surroundings and is hard to spot and attack.

  • Beyond 10", he can't be spotted (though he can be seen if someone standing closer points him out).
  • Closer, he counts as having a 20% chance to hide in shadows, without needing to stay still. Characters who can already hide in shadows get +20% if they stay still.
  • Missile weapons are -4 to hit him.

Material component: the shed skin of a small lizard.

The OA wu jen spell fiery eyes (OA p.75), for reference:

Element: Fire (OA Table 66).

The wu jen's eyes glow with unnatural fire, casting bright light 3 feet, as clear as a lantern.

  • Fixing his gaze on one spot for 3 rounds, he can make burnable things burst into small, flickering flames if he wishes.
  • Any creature looking at him saves versus spell; on a failure it hesitates an instant, fascinated, and automatically loses initiative next round.

The OA wu jen spell prestidigitation (OA p.76), for reference:

Sharpens the wu jen's manual dexterity and lets him teleport small objects to other points on his body.

  • Picking pockets: the victim saves versus spell. If he saves, the attempt is discovered, with whatever consequences follow; if he fails, the wu jen takes the item.
  • Palming: with a quick pass of the hand, things small enough to fit in his palm vanish and reappear elsewhere on his person (a pocket, a boot, the other hand), or come from elsewhere on his person into his hand. Onlookers save versus spell to notice.
  • Each trick takes only seconds, and several can be done in one round: he could pick up a rare gem, secretly move it to his hat and replace it with a cheap substitute from his pocket in a few seconds.

Material component: a small drop of oil rubbed on the fingertips.

The reverse, fumble-fingers, is cast on a victim within 3". For the duration, he must save versus spell to perform any action needing manual dexterity. It doesn't affect large actions such as melee, but can make an archer fumble his arrow, a ninja drop his tools, or a spellcaster confuse his gestures. Material component: a little oil sprinkled at the victim.

The OA wu jen spell disguise (OA p.82), for reference:

The wu jen takes on the look of any creature of his own species or sub-species, if he knows the person whose look he takes. It is a complete illusion of the new identity: face, build and even voice. It gives none of that person's abilities, habits or ways of thinking.

  • Observers who know the person have a 5% chance per level of the caster to see through it, noticing a change in his behavior. Those who don't know him or have met him only a few times accept it automatically. Actions wholly out of character let everyone present check whether the disguise is pierced.
  • The disguised person gives off a faint aura of magic, which detect magic can notice; detect illusion reveals the spell.

Material component: something from the body of the person copied (hair, nail clippings) or an item he always wears or carries, kept on the wu jen for the whole spell; if it is set aside, the spell ends at once. Important officials and powerful characters take great care disposing of things that could be used for such a disguise, such as burning cut hair and nail parings.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.82. Rewritten in plain words.

The OA wu jen spell face (OA p.82), for reference:

Creates the illusion that the wu jen is of higher social level, title, office or position than he is. He chooses which (social level, title or office), and it rises 1d4 ranks. He gains the confidence, air of power, manners, speech and etiquette of that rank.

  • On those unfamiliar with the rank it works especially well: they show him great respect, their encounter reactions are 10% better than the rank alone would give, and they unhesitatingly believe he holds the position and is very fearsome and powerful.
  • Those familiar with the rank save versus spell. If they fail, they treat him as having it. If they succeed, they notice small flaws in his behavior: after one turn they grow suspicious, and after two they realize he is an impostor. Whether they tell others, and what they do, depends on the situation.
  • Those of higher status also save, with the same results, and never treat him as an equal anyway.

Material component: a drop of honey.

The reverse, lose face, makes the victim socially graceless. He must be touched (normal hit roll) but gets no save. Neither he nor those with him notice any change at once, but whenever social graces matter, he somehow does the wrong thing, to the obvious notice of those around him. The DM judges the exact effect of such blunders by the situation and the non-player characters involved. Material component: a small piece of charcoal.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.82. Rewritten in plain words.

The OA wu jen spell smoke shape (OA p.80), for reference:

Element: Air (OA Table 66).

The wu jen shapes masses of smoke, mist or fog into any form he likes: a misty warrior, or thick smoke formed into a solid-looking wall. The shape keeps all the properties of smoke or fog, but holds its form in all conditions until the spell ends. Once it is finished, he can give it a gentle push, sending it in one direction at 3" a round. The detail is fine enough to fool onlookers at a distance, but not great. At the end it dissipates quickly. No material component is needed, but there must be a source of mist or smoke to work with: early morning fog, or a large smoky fire.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.80. Rewritten in plain words.

The OA wu jen spell memory (OA p.83), for reference:

Plants a false memory in the mind of an intelligent creature that understands the wu jen's speech. The victim saves versus spell, at -2 if unconscious or asleep.

  • After the brief casting, the wu jen goes on describing the memory. He can implant memories of events up to 1 turn long per level: a 12th level wu jen could build a memory of an event two hours long. The exact casting time is however long the description takes.
  • He gains limited knowledge of the victim's existing memories, only enough to fit the new one logically into the flow of events.
  • The new memory can replace one already there (changing how an encounter turned out, or the orders the victim received), or be wedged into a "blank space" (an encounter during an otherwise forgettable journey).
  • It has no magical force (it isn't a suggestion), but can be used to encourage friendliness or hostility, or change the victim's mission. The wu jen must take care to make memories logical, fitting the victim's personality or logically explained: telling an intelligent evil monster it likes a traditional enemy of its race simply because he was nice isn't enough; telling it that it likes the character because he spared its life is far more acceptable. If the DM rules the memory wholly out of character, the victim gets a second save at +4 at the end of the spell.

The reverse, erasement, removes any memory from the victim, with the same limits. The time erased is a blank to him; he has no idea what happened.

Dispel magic, remember or a similar spell removes an implanted memory or restores an erased one. Material components: a sheet of white paper, a brush and a pot of ink.

Dragon #130 p.16-20 (Len Carpenter, "Magic from East to West"); OA p.83. Rewritten in plain words.

The OA wu jen spell creeping darkness (OA p.88), for reference:

Element: Air (OA Table 66).

An amorphous cloud of inky blackness that the caster can shape and move as he likes for the duration, while he concentrates, within range, at 6" a round. It can seep through the smallest cracks and float in the air. No vision passes through it except true sight or similar spells, and it blots out all sound inside, so spellcasters in it can't cast spells that need speech. Wind affects it: for every five miles per hour of wind, the area shrinks by 1 cubic foot and the duration by one round. While concentrating, the wu jen can move no more than 3" a round. Material components: a whisker from an old black cat and a tiny bottle of smoke captured on a moonless night.

The OA wu jen spell summoning wind (OA p.95), for reference:

Element: Air (OA Table 66).

A magic wind carries an urgent message to one or more creatures. The wu jen phrases a message of 25 words or less, sent to up to 10 creatures per level of the caster. Their exact identities needn't be known, but some common identifier is needed, more specific than race or class: some identifier of position, such as the soldiers of his palace guard, or the governors of all the provinces of one land. It is delivered on a gentle breeze, whispering into the ears of those it is meant for. It doesn't compel them to answer or act, only tells them the message. It is often used to rally troops, send warnings or spread proclamations.
